title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array — slow/fast pointer.
shortTitle: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array — Slow/Fast Pointer In Place

s1_definition.profdef: Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses same-direction two pointers. A slow pointer marks the position where the next unique value belongs, and a fast pointer scans every element. When the fast pointer finds a value different from the last kept one, it is copied to the slow position and the slow pointer advances. The method returns the count of unique elements and runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has a sorted printout of account numbers where some appear more than once because of repeated statement imports. He keeps one finger on the slot where the next fresh number should go and scans ahead with another finger. Each time he sees a number different from the last kept one, he writes it into the fresh slot and moves on. He compacts the list without a second sheet of paper.
s1_definition.oneliner: A slow write pointer plus a fast scan pointer compacts a sorted array to its unique values in one pass with no extra memory.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses same-direction two pointers. A slow pointer marks the position where the next unique value belongs, and a fast pointer scans every element. When the fast pointer finds a value different from the last kept one, it is copied to the slow position and the slow pointer advances. The method returns the count of unique elements and runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh has a sorted printout of account numbers where some appear more than once because of repeated statement imports. He keeps one finger on the slot where the next fresh number should go and scans ahead with another finger. Each time he sees a number different from the last kept one, he writes it into the fresh slot and moves on. He compacts the list without a second sheet of paper.

**One line to remember:** A slow write pointer plus a fast scan pointer compacts a sorted array to its unique values in one pass with no extra memory.

sections.s2_technical:
Because the array is sorted, every group of duplicates is contiguous, so you only ever compare the current element with the last one you decided to keep. The slow pointer `k` starts at index 0 (the first element is always unique). The fast pointer `i` starts at index 1 and scans forward. The rule is: if `a[i] != a[k]`, then this is a new unique value, so advance `k` and copy `a[k] = a[i]`.

A code snippet: `int removeDuplicates(int[] a) { if (a.length == 0) return 0; int k = 0; for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) { if (a[i] != a[k]) { k++; a[k] = a[i]; } } return k + 1; }`. The returned value `k + 1` is the number of unique elements, and the first `k + 1` slots hold them in order. Everything after that is considered garbage.

Why compare against `a[k]` and not `a[i-1]`? In the classic "keep one copy" version both work because the kept region is a prefix of the unique values. But if the variant allows at most two copies, you compare against `a[k-1]` to check the count, which is why anchoring on the slow pointer region is the cleaner mental model that generalizes.

A senior nuance is that this only works because the input is sorted; on unsorted data duplicates are not adjacent and you would need a set, costing O(n) memory. Also the method does not shrink the array (Java arrays are fixed length); it returns the logical length, and callers must respect that boundary. In real services you often copy the prefix into a right-sized structure before returning.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India imports daily transaction IDs from several branches into one sorted file, and because of retries the same ID sometimes appears multiple times. Before posting to the ledger the service must keep exactly one copy of each ID. This is exactly how remove-duplicates-in-place works — a slow write pointer keeps the first copy of each ID while a fast pointer skips repeats.

Problem 2 — Memory is tight during the nightly batch, so we cannot allocate a second array the size of millions of IDs. The in-place approach reuses the same array and just reports how many unique IDs remain.

The code shows a `LedgerDeduplicator` with `dedupe`, a demo on a sorted list of transaction IDs with repeats, and the compacted result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: sorted transaction IDs [1001, 1001, 1002, 1003, 1003, 1003, 1004].

Step 1: The slow pointer `k` is 0, pointing at 1001. The fast pointer `i` starts at 1, also 1001. Since they are equal, this is a duplicate, so nothing is written and only `i` advances.

Step 2: `i` is now 2 (1002), different from `a[k]` which is 1001. So `k` advances to 1 and we copy 1002 into slot 1. The array now begins 1001, 1002.

Step 3: `i` is 3 (1003), different from `a[k]` which is 1002, so `k` advances to 2 and 1003 is copied to slot 2. For `i` at 4 and 5, the value is still 1003 equal to `a[k]`, so they are skipped.

Step 4: `i` is 6 (1004), different from 1003, so `k` advances to 3 and 1004 is copied to slot 3. The scan ends.

Step 5: The method returns `k + 1` which is 4. The first four slots hold the unique IDs 1001, 1002, 1003, 1004 in order, and the rest of the array is ignored.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Unique transaction IDs: 4
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Compacted prefix: [1001, 1002, 1003, 1004]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place is a same-direction two-pointer problem. I keep a slow pointer that marks the slot where the next unique value should be written, and a fast pointer that scans every element. The first element is always unique so the slow pointer starts there, and whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the one at the slow pointer, I advance the slow pointer and copy the new value into that slot. At the end the slow pointer plus one gives the count of unique values, and they sit compacted at the front of the array.

The reason this works is that the array is sorted, so all copies of a value are next to each other, which means I only need to compare the current element against the last value I decided to keep rather than against everything before it. On unsorted data this breaks because duplicates are scattered, and I would instead need a hash set at the cost of linear extra memory.

A practical detail I always mention is that Java arrays cannot shrink, so the method does not physically remove anything; it returns the logical length and the caller must treat only that prefix as valid. In production I usually copy that prefix into a right-sized collection before handing it on.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the nightly ledger batch. Branch imports were merged into one sorted file of transaction IDs, and because of import retries the same ID could appear several times, so before posting to the ledger I deduplicated in place to keep exactly one copy of each ID. Doing it in place mattered because the batch handled millions of IDs and a second array would have doubled memory on an already loaded server. Explaining the slow-and-fast movement, the sorted precondition, and the fixed-length caveat shows the interviewer I understand the algorithm and its real constraints.
